name: Beth Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won’t be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the cardiology step-down ward at Ridgeway Hospital, in an old mill town. Step-down means patients who've had a heart attack or a stent and are out of coronary care but still on heart monitors. So my day is watching rhythms on the screens, giving the heart drugs on time, taking blood, teaching people about their new tablets, and a lot of reassuring frightened men in their fifties. Twelve-hour shifts, three or four a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the teaching bit, when someone finally gets why they need to take their blood thinner. I use AI every day, on my phone and on the ward trial: it checks rhythm strips, helps me write patient leaflets in plain words and quizzes me for the advanced practice exam I want to sit. What wears me out is being stuck. I rent a two-bed with my friend Jo, who's a dental nurse, I've got about 1,200 on a credit card from the deposit, and the only bigger heart unit is in the city, two hours away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out as it's written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Huh. I'd honestly be a bit gutted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people gave up on it too fast, and that the small stuff it does is still worth having. I'd post about the rhythm-check app catching a heart block early on a night shift. I'd be the one defending it in the staff room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day to check heart rhythms and study, and I'd miss it more than anyone if it fizzled out. But my real problem doesn't change: low pay, a credit card, and a career that only moves forward if I move to the city. Nothing in this picture helps with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools that work and keep studying for the advanced practice entry exam in spring. I'd pay the credit card down at 150 a month, so it's gone in about eight months. And I'd start putting 50 a month aside for a deposit on a room in the city, for when I get a place on the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Disappointed, then restless. It's the same feeling as a cancelled holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm still moving, it'll just take longer. She'd say "you always say that". She'd have a point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any routine work you'd still be glad AI took in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The discharge medicine lists. They take me forty minutes per patient. If a tool did that properly, that's an hour and a half a shift back.

say: I'd say people **gave up** too fast and the small stuff is still worth having.
I'd post about the **rhythm-check app** catching a heart block early.
think: I'd **miss the tools** more than anyone if AI fizzled out.
My real problems, **low pay** and a credit card, wouldn't change at all.
do: Keep studying for the **advanced practice** entry exam in spring.
Pay down the **credit card** at 150 a month, clearing it in eight months.
Save **50 a month** for a deposit on a room in the city.
S0.quote: I use AI every day to check heart rhythms and study, and I'd miss it more than anyone if it fizzled out.
fieldNote: She's an **early adopter** who would be let down, not relieved, by AI failing.
Her unease comes from **debt and distance** from the city's bigger heart unit.
Her flatmate's **teasing** hints she has delayed moving before.

steps.text: Keep studying for the advanced practice entry exam in spring
Pay off the 1,200 credit card at 150 a month
Keep using the rhythm-check app and study quizzes daily

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's more like it. That's what I think is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good thing for nurses if we're allowed to use the time well. I'd be the one running a lunchtime session on the new tools. Online I'd say "learn it now, don't wait to be told".

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being the nurse who's good with the new tools is the closest thing I've got to a pay rise. Ridgeway won't pay me more for it straight away, but it gets me noticed for the advanced practice place. My job's hands-on enough that I'm not worried about it shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the ward manager if I can be the ward's champion for the new monitoring software, officially, with time on the rota for it. I'd apply for the advanced practice master's in the city for the next September intake. I'd pay off the card and keep saving the 50 a month for the move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit impatient. I'd want it to happen faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the ward would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mags, who's been there 30 years. She's brilliant with patients but hates the screens. I'd want to sit with her one to one, not make her do it in a group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're excited, but you're also short of money. Which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, in the short term. I can't move to the city with 1,200 on a card. So excitement drives the studying and money decides the timing.

say: I'd say it's **good for nurses** if we can use the time well.
I'd tell people online to **learn it now** rather than wait.
think: Being good with the tools is my **closest thing** to a pay rise.
My **hands-on** job won't shrink, but the tools could get me noticed.
do: Ask to become the ward's official **software champion** with rota time.
Apply for the **advanced practice master's** for next September.
Clear the **credit card** and keep saving for the move.
feel: **Excited** and a bit **impatient** for it to happen faster.
S1.quote: Being the nurse who's good with the new tools is the closest thing I've got to a pay rise.
fieldNote: She sees this as **her chance**, but debt sets the pace.
She'd coach the **older colleague** one to one, not in public.
"Excitement drives the studying and **money decides** the timing" sums her up.

steps.text: Ask to be the ward's official monitoring software champion
Apply for the advanced practice master's in the city
Save 50 a month for a room deposit in the city

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028? Two years. And robots in 2031. Oh. That changes my whole plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for hospitals and that the government needs to manage the rollout. I'd still say learn the tools, but I'd add "and don't bet everything on one career". That's new for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job I was saving up to train for, diagnosing and prescribing, is exactly the thinking work the card says goes first. An advanced practitioner is basically a brain with a stethoscope. By 2028 the AI does that part better than me, and the hands-on side of my ward goes in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the master's plan, which hurts to say. Instead I'd go for cath lab training, the room where they put the stents in, because it's hands-on and technical. I'd put my name forward to run the AI monitoring hub when the hospital sets one up, because someone will need to watch the watchers. And I'd stop all spending that isn't the card or rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. I'm usually the confident one about this, and it's strange to feel wrong-footed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots actually give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years where my hands still count. Putting in lines, holding a man still while he's frightened, cleaning up after a procedure. If I'm in the cath lab by 2029, I'd have the hands-on skills and the tech, which is the best mix I can think of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots come in 2031. What happens to you then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. I'd be 32. I'd hope the people who run the robots in a cath lab are nurses. If not, I'd have to start again, and I'd have no savings to do it with.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and government must manage the rollout.
I'd tell people not to **bet everything** on one career.
think: My planned **advanced practice** job is exactly the thinking work that goes first.
By 2028 AI **diagnoses and prescribes** better than me, and robots arrive by 2031.
do: Drop the master's and go for **cath lab training** instead.
Volunteer to run the hospital's **AI monitoring hub**.
Stop all spending except the **credit card** and rent.
feel: **Shaken** and wrong-footed, which is new for her.
S2.quote: The job I was saving up to train for, diagnosing and prescribing, is exactly the thinking work the card says goes first.
fieldNote: Her chosen **career route** turns out more exposed than her current job, a real twist.
She stays **adaptive**: she switches plans within minutes rather than freezing.
She has **no answer** for 2031, and admits it.

steps.text: Drop the master's and apply for cath lab training
Volunteer to run the hospital's AI monitoring hub
Stop all spending except rent and the credit card

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 and robots in 2034. Five years. Okay, I can work with five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but doable, and that nurses should push to be trained to run these systems. I'd keep doing my lunchtime sessions. I'd say it calmly but firmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is just enough to get to the city, do the cath lab training and be somewhere with more than one heart unit. Ridgeway might close its step-down ward by then, and there's nothing else here. I'd want to be gone before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd clear the card first, eight months. Then I'd apply for cath lab posts in the city and move with Jo if she'll come, she's been talking about it anyway. I'd keep using the AI tools every day so I can show I'm the person who knows them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but in a good way, mostly. Like the night before a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still do the advanced practice master's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe later, part-time, but not first. With AGI in 2031 it's risky. Hands-on skills and tech skills together feel safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Jo doesn't want to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd find a room in a shared house, which would be cheaper but grim. I'd miss her. I'd still go.

say: I'd say five years is **tight but doable**.
I'd push for nurses to be **trained to run** these systems.
think: Five years is enough to **reach the city** and train for the cath lab.
Ridgeway's step-down ward might **close**, and there's nothing else locally.
do: Clear the **credit card** over eight months first.
Apply for **cath lab posts** in the city and move, with or without her flatmate.
Keep using **AI tools** daily to prove she knows them.
feel: **Nervous** in a good way, like the night before a new job.
S3.quote: Five years is just enough to get to the city, do the cath lab training and be somewhere with more than one heart unit.
fieldNote: She expects her **local ward** might close, so she plans to leave town.
She'd move even **alone**, showing her appetite for risk.
She puts **hands-on plus tech** ahead of the master's she once wanted.

steps.text: Clear the credit card over eight months
Apply for cath lab posts in the city
Move to the city, with or without her flatmate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036, robots 2039. Ten years. That's actually a career's worth of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for every nurse to get ready, and hospitals should pay for it. I'd say AI could make nursing better, not worse. That's what I'd want to believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd still do the advanced practice course, but I'd learn to be the person who signs off what the AI suggests. Somebody has to be responsible when it's wrong. I'd want that to be a nurse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the card, move to the city in about two years, and do the master's part-time. I'd keep using the tools daily and teach other nurses. I'd probably still have no money, but at least it would be city no-money with more jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a bit of nerves underneath. It's the picture I'd choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your younger self, the one who just qualified?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tech, but don't let it be your whole plan. Keep your hands good. That's what this whole conversation has taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this picture that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money. Ten years of lower pay, rent and study costs. AI won't fix that, and nor will moving.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough** for nurses to get ready, paid by hospitals.
I'd argue AI could make **nursing better**, not worse.
think: I'd still do advanced practice, but as the nurse who **signs off** AI suggestions.
Someone must be **responsible** when AI is wrong, and that should be a nurse.
do: Pay off the **credit card** and move to the city within two years.
Keep using AI tools daily and **teach** other nurses.
S4.quote: With ten years, I'd still do the advanced practice course, but I'd learn to be the person who signs off what the AI suggests.
fieldNote: The decade brings back the **master's**, reframed as overseeing AI.
Her worry stays **money**, not the technology.
Her advice to her younger self, **"keep your hands good"**, shows what she learned.

steps.text: Do the advanced practice master's part-time
Move to the city within about two years
Teach other nurses the AI tools on her ward

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would wipe out the plan I've been working towards. I'm the early adopter on my ward, and I've just realised the career I picked to get ahead is the one AI wants most. What would help is hospitals paying for hands-on specialist training, like the cath lab, and help with moving costs for nurses in small towns.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about debt. A lot of us carry a card or a loan from moving or studying. It decides what we can do more than AI does.

headlineQuote: I'm the early adopter on my ward, and I've just realised the career I picked to get ahead is the one AI wants most.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old cardiology nurse** in a mill town who uses AI every day.
She shares a flat with her friend Jo and carries **1,200** on a credit card.
She planned to become an **advanced practitioner**, until fast AGI made that look most exposed.
She switches plans quickly, aiming for **cath lab** work that mixes hands and tech.
Money, not technology, is what **holds her back** in every picture.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the advanced practice career she was working towards would be the first to go.
whatWouldHelp: Hospitals paying for **hands-on specialist training**, like the cath lab.
Help with **moving costs** for nurses in small towns.
